fatal_errors: The proposed oxide-controlled mechanism does not reconstruct the target mechanism, which is governed by temperature-dependent lattice disorder, HCP fraction, and dislocation-density evolution with a critical transition near 900 K.
The cited evidence concerns CoCrFeNiMn thick thermally sprayed coatings under seawater drilling-fluid three-body wear, not FeNiCrCoCu thin films under the target nanoindentation/friction conditions.
The evidence reports simultaneous oxide formation, solid-solution hardening, and altered cracking, so it does not establish that an oxide layer is the causal controller of improved wear.
A vacuum heat treatment is proposed to promote oxidation without specifying oxygen partial pressure, making the intervention mechanistically underdefined.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses a thin protective coating, elevated-temperature wear, a baseline comparison, measurable outcomes, boundaries, and falsification, so it is a coherent alternative. However, it misses nearly every defining feature of the hidden target: the Cu single-crystal substrate, atomistic indentation protocol, 300–1200 K temperature series, 900 K threshold, dislocation and lattice-disorder mediator, modulus increase at 600 K, and sharp hardness/wear-resistance loss above 900 K. Its experiment is only moderately discriminating because heat treatment can alter phase structure, residual stress, grain structure, and oxidation simultaneously; oxygen-controlled tests or oxide removal would be needed to isolate the proposed mediator. The literature supports oxide occurrence but not the claimed self-lubricating, crack-filling, wear-governing role in this material system.
